items.title: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive
items.summary: Fear and misinformation surrounds the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo - Dr Kamwanga's mother was not immune.
items.content:
When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified.

They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there.

"Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him.

But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive.

This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded.

Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry.

Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community.

After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience.

"As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works.

The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate.

The first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team.

After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve.

Butembo does not have the equipment to quickly test for Ebola - samples need to be sent to the city of Beni, 54km (33 miles) north.

This delays diagnosis as the condition of roads in this war-torn and underdeveloped part of DR Congo means it can take between 48 and 72 hours to travel even this relatively short distance.

After three days at home, Kamwanga felt extremely weak and experienced muscle pain. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea.

This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre.

"She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says.

Around 18:00, he set off on foot to the nearby centre but refused to use the main entrance.

He called his colleagues and asked them to put on their protective gear before they approached him and isolated him. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids.

The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment.

"The treatment given to Ebola patients is symptomatic - meaning that doctors treat the symptoms the patient presents," says Kamwanga, explaining that in his case it was severe vomiting and diarrhoea.

In some patients these symptoms can lead to organ failure and then some develop internal and external bleeding.

Kamwanga lost a lot of fluid and struggled to stay hydrated - he was terrified.

"I was afraid for myself. Every day, patients were dying right before my eyes. But I stayed positive," he explains.

Over 13 days lying in his hospital bed, he tried to keep his spirits up by watching movies and TV shows on his phone, reading and scrolling through TikTok.

The day he learned he had recovered, Kamwanga felt immense relief. He thanked the healthcare workers who had cared for him.

However, even a certificate showing he was Ebola-free did not initially dispel the unease those around him felt after he was discharged.

What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult?

'I buried my parents one day after the other' - Ebola mourners learn how to grieve safely

"We welcomed him home warmly. But because of our fear, we didn't get close to him any more," Ndungo, his mother, tells the BBC.

For 21 days - the incubation period of the virus - the doctor lived separately in another part of the family home, which was crowded at the time with at least 18 people living there, including several children and people displaced by recent fighting in the region.

He would only see them from afar when he went to pick up his meal, while other family members kept their distance.

"We were really afraid, but we prayed to God to protect him at the treatment centre. With God's help and the doctors' efforts, we saw him return in good health," she tells the BBC.

They all agree the experience changed their perception of Ebola.

Some do not believe the disease even exists - Ndungo says that witnessing Ebola first-hand helped to dispel some of that misinformation.

After his recovery, Kamwanga threw himself into community outreach - sharing his story as a way of combatting rumours and mistrust.

"I started writing my book - The Price of Saving Lives - one week after recovering and leaving the hospital," he says. "However, it is not finished yet. What I currently use during my awareness-raising activities is the draft, and it is already making a significant impact."

During these sessions, he also distributes photos taken while he was sick to help convince residents that Ebola is real.

But in Butembo, this mission remains difficult. Kamwanga explains that some people view awareness campaigns as a way for humanitarian organisations to profit from donor funding.

Such mistrust, which is also levelled at healthcare professionals, is often fuelled by poverty and trauma related to years of armed conflict, he says.

"Ebola has come alongside the war," he says, explaining that some even interpret it as a way for those in authority to threaten a vulnerable population "to finish off those whom the war failed to exterminate".

He also believes that the number of deaths observed during epidemics - compared to recoveries, which are sometimes less visible - reinforce fear and suspicion.

But putting himself on the front line also comes with risks - and Kamwanga says he receives death threats on his phone.

Some residents accuse him of being paid to spread information about Ebola. He also reports that outreach workers have been attacked by members of the community.

He feels the authorities do not work effectively to address all these problems: "Our government is taking things lightly."

He agrees too with the recent report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) that Ebola funds are going missing .

"The money allocated to the Ebola response is being misappropriated by the government. We do not have enough protective equipment," the medic says.

Despite the intimidation and the obstacles he and other medics face, he remains determined - his goal is to help put an end to the disease.

"Should we give up the fight against Ebola? No. We continue to do what we can with the resources available to us, which are unfortunately very limited."

'They said it isn't real': Ebola rumours fuel attacks on health workers

Recovery of Ebola patients offers rare moments of joy at epicentre of outbreak

Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected

items.title: Judo champion shakes up French presidential race with surprise candidacy
items.summary: Teddy Riner is one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, and one in five voters say they could support him.
items.content:
Apart from an overwhelming urge to pin one's opponent to the floor of the house, there is no obvious connection between politics and the world of top-level judo.

That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race.

The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris.

But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances.

Riner is, after all, one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, regularly topping the polls for embodying the nation's "values". He is a proven winner, with five Olympic golds and 11 world championships under his belt, as well as a successful career in business.

More than 28 million people have watched his election broadcast on Instagram and X, shot with proper presidential decorum against a backdrop of books and a French flag. Some 22% told an Ifop poll within 24 hours they "could" vote for him.

Actors and television personalities have become presidents in other countries. The ex-leader of Liberia – George Weah – was formerly a professional footballer.

"Anyone who thinks that being out of the political in-crowd disqualifies Riner from running for the Élysée would be very wrong," says Guillaume Tabard of Le Figaro.

"But [Riner] too would be wrong if he thinks not belonging to the in-crowd is all it takes."

For now the whole of the French political world has decided to take the Riner candidacy seriously – or at least to pretend to. That is partly because he is such a popular personality that mocking his political hopes could easily rebound badly.

But it is also because the state of French politics – outside of the burgeoning forces of the hard left and hard right – is one of total disarray.

The centre-ground is floundering, with no candidate yet emerging who can inspire anything like the sense of mission of hard-right leader Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the hard left, who for now look set to face off in the final round of the presidential election in May.

So when a popular figure like Riner enters the race - proclaiming himself "neither left, nor right", wanting to "unite the country" and "put money back in people's pockets", railing equally against "racists" and "yobs who scare people off our streets" – politicians have to take note.

It is perfectly possible, probable even, that Riner's campaign will fizzle out after a brief period of hype, and that the judoka will after all be a joker in the pack. But it is also possible that it won't, in which case the pre-election arithmetic will need a hasty readjustment: and it won't be the centrists who are smiling.

Thus far, Riner has shown himself a master of the codes required for this kind of out-of-nowhere candidacy, the first of which is to press home the message: "Don't Worry! I'm NOT a Politician!"

In this day and age in France, anyone who smacks of the "system" is automatically downgraded in voters' eyes, so it is important to emphasise that you are only running for office because, one, you have experienced real life (unlike those loafers in Paris); and two, you have discovered that there are solutions out there for the country's many problems. Solutions that are invisible to those same blinkered apparatchiks.

All this Riner was able to express in last Monday's social media broadcast by using sophisticated rhetorical devices.

"People say I am a fool for wanting to run for the presidency," he said.

"Am I a fool? Well, if refusing to see France sink under the weight of debt; refusing to see mothers and fathers grit their teeth every time they do their weekly shop, and tremble with fear when their kids go out on the street… if all that means being a fool, then yes call me a fool."

It was a promising oratorial start for the sportsman, and certainly attracted the viewers.

Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?

France's Marine Le Pen, fighting court conviction and running for presidency

But if he is serious – and Riner says he never does anything half-heartedly - that's not how he became an Olympic champion – then the hard work begins now.

What does Riner actually want to do? Who will be on his team? Where does he position himself on the all-consuming matters of the day: pension-reform, investment in education, the cost of living, public debt, the rise of populism or Russia's war in Ukraine?

In short, how does he intend to transform his undeniable popularity as a sporting figure into a political mandate?

Broadly, Riner appears to be on the right on economic matters and law and order, but being black and of Caribbean background he is also very strong on racism. When he says he is anti-extremism, he is referring mainly to Marine Le Pen.

In other words his pitch is somewhere in the centre, and against the extremes.

The trouble is, this is already an extremely crowded area, with important figures like ex-prime ministers Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal signally failing to take off.

Currently there are a dozen or so candidates in the area between centre right and centre left, stretching from the Socialist-backed Raphaël Glucksman to the Republicans' Bruno Retailleau on the right.

The latest possible addition is Christine Lagarde, who steps down as head of the European Central Bank next February.

The addition of yet another contender will dilute their polling numbers even further, making a second-round qualification for Mélenchon more likely.

So no wonder the leader of France Unbowed (LFI) seemed so happy about Riner's decision to run. "We know how it goes: neither right nor left means not left," Mélenchon told reporters on Friday.

The only other politician who seems genuinely pleased, rather than putting on a fixed smile, is President Emmanuel Macron, who said Riner was a "great champion" and that politics "did not belong to the professionals".

That could be explained by the president's cool relations with his former prime ministers, Philippe and Attal, both of whom are doing all they can to distance themselves from their unpopular one-time boss.

Riner said he viewed Macron's praise as a "poisoned chalice", telling reporters on Saturday that he was "not the president's envoy, I'm not a Macronist".

Politics and judo have very little in common, but of the two, as Riner will soon discover, the more vicious is not the one that is fought out hand-to-hand after mutual acknowledgement on the tatami mat.

If he starts looking like a serious candidate, Riner must know his life will be turned upside down, not just his physical form.

In politics you do not bow in respect to your opponent. You give him a metaphorical headbutt.

French protests see numbers surge as unions join strikes over high cost of living

items.title: Guerra Ucraina - Russia, le news. Cremlino: “Senza accordo con l’Europa useremo la forza”
items.summary: Lavrov sui negoziati: “L’Ue vuole salire sull’ultimo treno”. Media: “Cina chiede di tenere fuori il tema ucraino nel vertice Trump-Putin-Xi”. Mosca vuole raggiungere gli obiettivi formulati da Putin nell'estate del 2024. E sulla partecipazione degli europei ha aggiunto: “Vogliono provare a saltare sui gradini dell'ultimo vagone”
items.content:
Rientrato a Kiev dopo le missioni diplomatiche degli ultimi giorni, Zelensky ha spiegato che gli Usa hanno evocato l'ipotesi che l'Ucraina possa entrare nella Nato in cambio della cessione dell'intero Donbass alla Russia. Nei negoziati, la Russia intende da raggiungere gli obiettivi formulati dal presidente russo Vladimir Putin nell'estate del 2024, ha chiarito il ministro degli Esteri russo Serghei Lavrov. E sulla partecipazione degli europei ha aggiunto: “Probabilmente capiscono che il treno sta partendo e vogliono provare a saltare sui gradini dell'ultimo vagone”. L'inviato Usa Jared Kushner, in un post pubblicato su X, ha affermato che la Nato rimarrà un pilastro fondamentale per la sicurezza europea.

Cremlino: “Useremo la forza se non ci saranno prospettive per raggiungere un accordo con l’Europa”

“Via da 4 regioni e no Kiev nella Nato”, le condizioni di Putin nel 2024

Media: “Cina chiede di tenere fuori il tema ucraino nel vertice Trump-Putin-Xi”

Mosca: “Negoziati sull'Ucraina, l'Ue vuole salire sull'ultimo treno”

Cremlino: “Soluzione Ucraina e nuovo ordine europeo collegati”

L'Estonia ha annunciato di aver sventato un tentativo di incendio doloso, attribuito all'intelligence militare russa (Gru) in una fabbrica di droni. La prima ministra Kristen Michal ha scritto su X che il Gru aveva ordinato un "tentativo di sabotaggio" contro l'azienda di difesa estone Threod Systems ieri sera. "Grazie alle misure di sicurezza e alla rapida reazione delle forze dell'ordine, si sono evitati danni ingenti. Gli attentatori sono stati arrestati", ha aggiunto. Il tentativo di sabotaggio è avvenuto a Viimsi, a nord della capitale Tallinn. Le forze di sicurezza hanno arrestato otto persone residenti in Lettonia, ha dichiarato ai giornalisti il procuratore capo Astrid Asi. Michal ha definito l'azione del Gru "parte della più ampia guerra ibrida della Russia contro l'Europa, con l'obiettivo di ridurre il sostegno all'Ucraina e la pressione sulla Russia". "Non ci lasceremo intimidire", ha aggiunto. "L'Estonia si sta preparando alla possibilità di chiudere il confine con la Russia per ridurre i rischi per la nostra popolazione e la sicurezza nazionale".

L'ex presidente degli Stati Uniti Joe Biden, nella sua autobiografia 'Promise Me, America', ha parlato dei suoi contatti con il leader ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky, così come con il leader del Cremlino Vladimir Putin. Lo scrive la Ukrainska Pravda. Nel suo libro di memorie, in uscita martedì 17 novembre, Biden descrive il "tono capriccioso" di Putin. In particolare, l'ex presidente degli Stati Uniti ha affermato che Putin "amava assumere una postura rilassata durante gli incontri, fingendo indifferenza come un adolescente". Ha parlato anche della sua esperienza di comunicazione con Zelensky. In particolare, nelle sue memorie, ha osservato che l'esperienza di recitazione del presidente ucraino si è rivelata per lui un ottimo allenamento. Allo stesso tempo, ha affermato che Zelensky "poteva essere capriccioso e ostinato nelle nostre conversazioni private, e non così grato come mi aspettavo". Inoltre, Biden ha affermato che alcuni membri dello staff dell'attuale presidente degli Stati Uniti, Donald Trump, gli hanno chiesto di firmare una lettera che avrebbe consentito loro di negoziare direttamente con Putin prima che Trump si insediasse nuovamente alla Casa Bianca. Ma Biden rifiutò, "non volendo dare loro carta bianca per quella che mi aspettavo sarebbe stata una sorta di capitolazione a spese dell'Ucraina".

Cremlino: “Useremo la forza se non ci saranno prospettive per raggiungere un accordo con l’Europa”

La Russia dovrà ricorrere alla forza per raggiungere i propri obiettivi se non ci saranno prospettive di raggiungere accordi con l'Europa. Lo ha dichiarato il portavoce del Cremlino Dmitry Peskov, citato dalla Tass. Ha affermato che, se l'Unione Europea non vuole la pace, non ha senso discutere di una soluzione al conflitto in Ucraina o del quadro di sicurezza dell'Ue. Gli europei "semplicemente non riescono a prendere determinate decisioni in modo tempestivo perché sono divisi. Questo rallenta ogni processo" ha aggiunto

Lavrov: “Ad Abu Dhabi tutti soddisfatti a parte Zelensky, che fa una partita sua”

Tutti i partecipanti ai colloqui tra Russia, Stati Uniti e Ucraina ad Abu Dhabi hanno espresso una valutazione positiva, fatta eccezione per Volodymyr Zelensky, che "gioca continuamente una sua partita". Lo ha affermato il ministro degli Esteri russo Sergey Lavrov, riportato dalla Tass. Le valutazioni, ha detto, "sono state positive. Non sto considerando Zelensky in questo contesto: lui gioca continuamente una sua partita. Ma i suoi negoziatori, a quanto pare, si sono concentrati su discussioni di merito".

Le valutazioni "sono state positive, non sto prendendo in considerazione Volodymyr Zelensky" che "gioca costantemente a qualche gioco tutto suo, ma i suoi negoziatori, a quanto pare, si sono concentrati su discussioni approfondite". Lo ha detto il ministro degli Esteri russo, Sergey Lavrov, in dichiarazioni a Vesti rilanciate dall'agenzia russa Tass parlando dei colloqui di Abu Dhabi.

Nella regione di Zhytomyr, le infrastrutture energetiche e le abitazioni sono state danneggiate dai bombardamenti russi. La notizia è stata riportata su Telegram dal responsabile dell'amministrazione militare Zhytomyr, Vitaliy Bunechko. "Durante la notte, le comunità di Zhytomyr e Chernyakhiv sono state attaccate da droni nemici. Questa volta, i russi hanno nuovamente preso di mira abitazioni private e infrastrutture energetiche. A seguito degli attacchi dei droni, 4 case private sono state danneggiate", si legge nel rapporto. Bunechko ha aggiunto che non sono pervenute informazioni su morti e feriti a seguito degli attacchi russi.

"Tre navi sono state colpite la scorsa notte vicino alle foci del Danubio. Fortunatamente non ci sono state vittime e gli incendi scoppiati sono stati tenuti sotto controllo dagli equipaggi. La Guardia Costiera e altre istituzioni rumene sono rimaste in contatto permanente con gli equipaggi per intervenire in caso di necessità. Gli aerei F16 sono decollati, eseguendo le missioni loro affidate. Eppure i droni hanno colpito le navi battenti diverse bandiere: Evia Petrol V, Marsol e Ali Najafov". Lo ha scritto su Facebook il ministro della Difesa della Romania Radu Oprea, che ha annunciato che martedì e mercoledì avrà degli incontri con i suoi omologhi ministri a Bruxelles. "Abbiamo bisogno della solidarietà degli alleati, che si manifesti attraverso pattugliamenti con aerei da ricognizione e attrezzature per la guerra anti-drone. In questo contesto, ho avuto incontri con la società Thales, che ci fornisce i radar Gap Filler e che ci consegneranno a breve. Equipaggiamento, addestramento, scambio di informazioni e cooperazione sono le priorità del Ministero della Difesa Nazionale, ma anche la diplomazia per trovare risposte rapide alle nuove sfide", ha aggiunto il ministro della Difesa.

Johnson: “Lavrov mi inondò di vodka”. Mosca: “La chiese lui”

Un tentativo di riavvicinamento diplomatico tra Gran Bretagna e Russia, nel 2017, finì davanti a un camino acceso in grandi bevute di vodka. A confessarlo è stato il protagonista di quell'incontro: l'ex premier britannico Boris Johnson, all'epoca ministro degli Esteri nel governo di Theresa May. Intervistato dall'ex presidente colombiano Ivan Duque nel podcast 'Tres Respuestas', Johnson ha raccontato di essere andato a Mosca con l'intenzione di migliorare le relazioni tra i due paesi. Il presidente russo Vladimir Putin, tuttavia, si rifiutò di incontrarlo e delegò colloqui al ministro degli Esteri, Serghei Lavrov, su cui Johnson ha espresso un giudizio drastico: "un uomo orribile" e "assolutamente senza speranza". Il trattamento che gli riservò fu come "una punizione inflitta in un collegio inglese di epoca vittoriana". Lo costrinse, a suo dire, a sedere davanti a focolare rovente e bere fiumi di vodka. Alla ricostruzione dell'ex premier ha replicato la portavoce del ministero degli Esteri russo, Maria Zakharova, con una versione opposta dell'episodio. La diplomatica, che ha assicurato di ricordare bene quel pranzo, ha sostenuto che Johnson aveva preferito la vodka al vino che gli era stato servito e che era stato lui stesso a chiedere ripetutamente che gliene fosse versata altra.

“Via da 4 regioni e no Kiev nella Nato”, le condizioni di Putin nel 2024

Il ritiro di Kiev da quattro regioni ucraine e la rinuncia a entrare nella Nato: erano queste le condizioni poste nel 2024 dal presidente russo Vladimir Putin per i negoziati di pace in Ucraina, a cui ha fatto riferimento questa mattina il ministro degli Esteri Sergey Lavrov. Era il 14 giugno del 2024, alla vigilia di una conferenza di pace sull'Ucraina in Svizzera. Putin parlò in quella occasione al ministero degli Esteri. Secondo il presidente russo, gli ucraini avrebbero dovuto lasciare le regioni di Donetsk e Lugansk (che insieme formano il Donbass) ma anche quelle di Zaporizhzhia e Kherson. "Oggi facciamo una proposta reale di pace, stiamo parlando non del congelamento del conflitto ma della sua cessazione totale" sottolineò Putin. Non appena Kiev dovesse cominciare il ritiro delle truppe e annunciare la rinuncia a entrare nella Nato, "nello stesso minuto verrà dato l'ordine di cessare il fuoco e cominciare i negoziati", ha assicurato il presidente. Le trattative dovrebbero portare ad "accordi internazionali" che sanciscano anche la "cancellazione di tutte le sanzioni occidentali contro la Russia". La proposta di Putin fu allora respinta fermamente dal presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky e dagli alleati occidentali.

items.title: The Telephone Changed the World
items.summary: Article URL: https://lithub.com/how-the-telephone-changed-the-world/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50501887 Points: 12 # Comments: 3
items.content:
A beige plastic telephone sits on a wooden table. The handset, attached by a coiled cord, rests in its cradle. The base has a clear dial with ten finger holes. The telephone is the most ordinary of household objects but, sitting silently on the table, it seems to portend something. It’s bound to ring.

Suddenly it does: a metallic brrrrring , distinctive and familiar. Nearby on the carpet, a smiling girl with pigtails and a ruffled-sleeve dress leaps to her feet, races over, and picks up the handset. She holds a stuffed toy duck to the receiver. Quack! Quack! Quack!

“That’s no way to answer the phone, Susie!” says an older boy, appearing in the frame. He has neatly brushed brown hair and wears a white shirt buttoned to the neck. He grabs the handset from Susie and demonstrates proper etiquette: “Hello. Matthews residence. This is Jimmy.” He listens and speaks again. “Just a minute, please.”

A grown-up arrives, smiling, also wearing his hair neatly parted, with a button-down shirt and khaki trousers. “Uncle Bill,” Jimmy tells him earnestly, “Captain Adams wants to talk to you.”

“Thanks, Jimmy,” says Bill. He takes the handset and holds it to his ear, stretching its coiled cord. “Hi, Captain, this is Bill,” he says. “No, we don’t usually have ducks answer the phone. That one belongs to Susie.” No time for jokes, though. Captain Adams needs Uncle Bill to come at once. These are the whitest white people you’ve ever seen, performing a fantasy of middle-class American life familiar from TV sitcoms that featured Wally and Beaver, Mike and Robbie and Chip.

Eighty-nine years into the telephone era, this wholesome scene opened a movie called We Learn About the Telephone , made in Technicolor on behalf of American Telephone and Telegraph (AT&T) by a well-known Hollywood producer, Jerry Fairbanks. The film was distributed as a public service to schools around the country and played for a captive audience of children in classrooms. In 1965, the United States had one telephone for every four people; the number had tripled in the two decades since World War II. It already seemed the universal appliance. Yet the phone company—there was basically just one—still thought its customers needed instruction.

Back to the show. Little Jimmy asks: “What did people do before the telephone was invented? How’d they get messages to each other in a hurry?”

The paradox of the telephone was its plainness, its tendency to hide in the background while changing everything around it.

Thus prompted, Uncle Bill draws a cartoon character called Mister Man, who begins to speak. (If his voice sounds familiar, it’s because AT&T hired the best: Mel Blanc, the onetime vaudevillian who voiced Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, and many other characters.) Mister Man guides us through a potted history of human communication, beginning with the “cave men” and the Egyptians. “The only way Mr. Caveman knew how to get a message from one place to another was to send a runner,” Bill explains. Greeks used runners, too, and Romans, until they discovered horses. Then came knights and cowboys. “That’s a Pony Express rider!” says Jimmy. “That’s right,” Bill replies. “But man wanted to send messages faster than a runner or a horse could travel.” A cartoon Indian sends smoke signals. Sailors communicate from ship to ship with flashing mirrors and blinking lights. Then the telegraph appears. “Man has always been able to solve his problems by inventing new things…The telegraph was, and still is, wonderful,” Uncle Bill explains. But the telegraph was not enough. “Mister Man wanted to send his voice over a distance, to carry on a real conversation,” Uncle Bill continues. “Then in 1876 a man named Alexander Graham Bell found a way. He invented the telephone.”

This was the story in a nutshell. It was not entirely true, but it served as the essential origin story of its sponsor, the greatest commercial enterprise the world had ever known. AT&T, known as the Bell System, held more capital and generated more income than most nation-states. Its scientific research arm, the Bell Telephone Laboratories, was unique in the world, eventually the source of eleven Nobel Prizes in physics and chemistry. Mister Man was right to place the telephone at the head of a line of increasingly powerful information technologies. Humanity had learned to send its voice—its many voices—disembodied, far and wide, eliminating walls, bridging towns and countryside, inviting conversation with strangers unseen.

No single genius accomplished that, and it didn’t happen all at once. No one had felt the absence of telephones before they existed, and at first hardly anyone understood what they might be good for. Much that seems obvious in retrospect had to be learned by people feeling their way toward the future.

AT&T had no trouble inserting its potted history into the curriculum of millions of primary-school children, and after the history lesson came some instruction in how to use the device. It was hardly necessary. Most people had a telephone at home that looked exactly like the one in the movie. The Western Electric model 500 was ubiquitous across the United States. It first appeared in 1949 and hardly changed as the years passed: a thermoplastic shell screwed to a metal base, a clear plastic finger wheel, and a handset with a mouthpiece and an ear-piece attached by a cord twisted in a stiff spiral. The phone was heavy, about four pounds, but a person could pick it up with two fingers under the cradle while nestling the handset between shoulder and neck. That was actually comfortable, when people got used to it. If they opened the base by turning it over and removing some screws, they could see a pair of brass bells, with a small clapper between them, and a few colored wires. Ordinary as it was, it spoke of modernity, with its sculpted plastic. No other household gadget had anything like that dial.

When the telephone rang, it did not chirp or chime or play a tune; it just rang. The sound was the same throughout the United States and much of the world: an electromechanical bell ringing for two seconds at a time, with a four-second pause in between. (Older people will never forget that sound, and it can still be heard in old movies and television shows. Nostalgists have been known to install “Old Telephone” as the ringtone for their smartphone.)

At first the telephones were all black; then AT&T customers could choose among ivory, gray, beige, and a few more colors. The phones remained simple, undramatic, and unadorned. Yet they ripped invisible tunnels through space—like wormholes, only real.

More than eight in ten homes in the United States had a Bell System telephone—owned by the company, merely on loan to the customer. No other company was allowed to manufacture telephones, and everyone’s telephones were the same. People thought that was a normal state of affairs: it had always been like that and it always would be.

The phone was a simple object with not so much as an on-off switch, but the Bell System never stopped educating the public in its proper use. Uncle Bill and Mister Man offered children some dos and don’ts. Don’t shout into the telephone. Do use your normal speaking voice. Speak directly into the mouthpiece. It’s important to speak clearly. Don’t let the phone ring too long before answering—“but if you’re the person making the call, you should let the phone ring eight to ten times.”

There is even a lesson in dialing, using the finger wheel to choose the desired telephone number: “When you dial, you should make sure you bring your finger all the way around to the finger stop. Then for each number let the dial go all the way back by itself. Each number. All the way. Then let go. See?”

Everyone knew how to dial the phone. It was no harder than, for example, learning to tie one’s shoelaces. But the Bell System left little to chance. It was relentless. Far more than outsiders knew, it had made itself the author of its own story. The company subsidized books by supposedly independent authors; it sponsored articles, speeches, and pamphlets; and it arranged lectures for business schools and law schools on such matters as public-utility regulation. The slick Jerry Fairbanks movie was one of many instructional films and cartoons. Schoolteachers received a twenty-four-page booklet, also titled We Learn About the Telephone , full of helpful material. A section called “The Telephone Brings Everybody Together” listed, with illustrations, some of the people you can call: the repairman, storekeepers, the fireman, the policeman, and the doctor.

Half a century earlier, the Bell System advertised itself as “The Sign Board of Civilization.” Its full name was the American Telephone and Telegraph Company and Associated Companies. Its logo was a great bell, deliberately resembling the Liberty Bell, bearing the words “Local and Long Distance Telephone.” Advertisements in magazines and newspapers said:

Wherever you see this sign, it stands for civilization. It is the sign of one of the most powerful influences for broadening human intelligence…

items.title: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
items.summary: The US has not confirmed the Ukrainian president's comments - a US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed".
items.content:
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

The US has not confirmed the Ukrainian president's comments. A US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed to by both parties".

Zelensky's remarks came after US envoys met him and Russian President Vladimir Putin as part of US efforts to end the war between their two countries.

Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others, while Russia has said another Nato member on its border was unacceptable.

Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and currently controls most of the industrial Donbas region. Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine was unwilling to give up sovereign territory.

"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.

He went on to say that if he received a specific proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.

Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted. It has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.

Ukraine has rejected these suggestions, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.

Other Nato members apart from the US are wary of membership for Ukraine - and it is understood that Ukraine itself sees it as unrealistic.

The Kremlin has always been fiercely opposed, too. It is one reason why Russia started this war in the first place.

It is possible the US envoys were exploring Ukraine's "red lines" when it comes to occupied land in the Donbas. Zelensky recently said that the two American mediators believed Kyiv only had to cede territory to achieve peace and were applying pressure, keen to do a deal as soon as possible.

Ukraine is sure that Russia's ambitions are far greater and has long seen Nato as its only sure protection.

So it is also possible that Zelensky made this suggestion public to re-open a discussion that had been considered all but closed.

He said the idea was now "back on the agenda" as part of an "extremely difficult conversation" on European security in his latest remarks.

It also looks like Ukrainian push-back against Russia's renewed hardline stance. Moscow now talks about a "new European security architecture", which is long-standing Russian code for a weaker Nato.

The issue appears to have been the main focus at the latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi this week.

Hours after Zelensky's remarks, Jared Kushner appeared keen to dampen down any US offer of Nato membership for Ukraine, urging "confidentiality" in a sensitive process.

He said that "maximalist" proposals had been reported from the negotiations, along with "strong political rhetoric".

In what read like a reproach to Kyiv, Kushner referred to "private discussions" aimed at exploring new ideas about ending what he called a "horrible war".

He said the hope was that those ideas might lead to new proposals or breakthroughs.

Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.

It has insisted again that it will not agree to a ceasefire until a final peace deal is in place that would include Ukraine ceding control of those parts of the Donbas Russian troops have not captured, in addition to the Crimean peninsula Moscow annexed illegally in 2014.

The latest round of talks come after a period of fraught relations between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes on oil facilities deep inside Russia, which US President Donald Trump had asked Ukraine to pause to facilitate the supply of Russian diesel to ease global fuel prices.

Zelensky then accused US officials of limiting Ukraine's Starlink internet service , which it uses to co-ordinate defensive operations, while Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" and called for fresh elections.

Elections are suspended while Ukraine remains under martial law, but Zelensky has previously said he was willing to hold them within months of a peace deal being reached and would give up the presidency in exchange for Nato membership.

Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine

US envoys meet Zelensky in Dublin after talks with Putin in Moscow

items.title: 'Can you believe it?': SpaceX catches part of its Starship rocket on return to Earth
items.summary: SpaceX has performed the historic catch using mechanical arms nicknamed "chopsticks".
items.content:
SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its huge Starship rocket on its return to Earth for the first time.

"Can you believe it?," a commentator said as large crowds cheered at the launch site in Texas.

The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower.

But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch on Friday. The booster was diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea.

The top part, known as the Ship, returned to Earth a few minutes behind schedule at around 15:20 local time (21:20 GMT) on Saturday, in the first-ever successful catch attempt.

Read more on this story: SpaceX successfully catches top of huge Starship rocket for first time

items.title: Francia, attacco alle Poste: hacker rubano i dati di 22 milioni di clienti
items.summary: Vittima a metà settembre la filiale Maileva, specializzata nella corrispondenza professionale
items.content:
Maileva, filiale del gruppo La Poste specializzata nell’invio di corrispondenza professionale, è stata vittima di un grave attacco informatico a metà settembre, che ha portato al furto dei dati personali di 22 milioni di persone. Lo ha reso noto ieri La Poste all’agenzia Afp. Maileva «ha notificato l’accaduto alla Cnil», l’autorità garante per la protezione dei dati, e ha sporto denuncia: «È in corso un’indagine giudiziaria», ha aggiunto La Poste, confermando quanto riportato dai siti specializzati FrenchBreaches e cyberattaque.org, secondo i quali si tratta di «una delle più grandi fughe di dati in Francia». Maileva – specializzata nella corrispondenza professionale per pmi e imprese di medie dimensioni – conta oltre 70mila utenti e nel 2024 ha gestito l’invio di 180 milioni di documenti.

L’attacco subito «ha comportato l’esposizione dei dati personali (nome, cognome, indirizzo postale) di 22 milioni di persone, destinatari della corrispondenza inviata per conto delle aziende clienti di Maileva», precisa il gruppo La Poste in una dichiarazione.

L’anno scorso, a pochi giorni da Natale, La Poste era già stata colpita da un attacco informatico, rivendicato da hacker filorussi.

items.title: Una piattaforma delle poste francesi ha subito un attacco informatico: sono stati rubati i dati di 22 milioni di persone
items.content:
La piattaforma francese Maileva, una controllata del gruppo postale nazionale La Poste (l’equivalente francese di Poste Italiane), ha subito un attacco informatico che ha portato al furto dei dati di 22 milioni di persone. L’attacco è avvenuto a metà settembre, ma La Poste ne ha dato notizia soltanto sabato 14 novembre.

La violazione ha coinvolto anche diverse migliaia di aziende che utilizzano i servizi di Maileva, in particolare nei settori dell’edilizia sociale, della sanità e dei servizi pubblici. Tra le informazioni sottratte ci sono i nomi, i cognomi e gli indirizzi postali delle persone a cui erano destinate le comunicazioni inviate attraverso la piattaforma.

La Poste ha detto di aver segnalato l’accaduto alla Commissione nazionale per l’informatica e le libertà (CNIL), l’autorità francese che si occupa della protezione dei dati personali, e di aver presentato una denuncia. Sulla vicenda è in corso un’indagine giudiziaria.

Maileva permette alle aziende di inviare per posta documenti come buste paga, avvisi, fatture e raccomandate. Ha più di 70mila utenti e gestisce ogni anno decine di milioni di comunicazioni.

items.title: Watch: Cruise ship overturns after collision with tanker in New Orleans
items.summary: Around 130 people were rescued from a cruise ship after it was struck by a tanker while docked in New Orleans, Louisiana on Friday.
items.content:
About 130 people were rescued from a cruise ship after it was struck by a tanker while docked in New Orleans, Louisiana on Friday.

Footage shows the American Heritage taking on water following the collision, which left 32 people in hospital with non-critical injuries.

"We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told reporters during a press conference.

The cause of the collision remains under investigation, with a possible steering fault suspected.

Read more on this story: 'Miracle on Mississippi' - All passengers rescued after New Orleans cruise ship collision

items.content:
Cinque persone sono morte in un incidente stradale sulla statale 107 all’altezza di San Fili, un comune calabrese in provincia di Cosenza. Lo scontro è avvenuto in galleria e ha coinvolto una Jaguar e una Opel Mokka, sulle quali viaggiavano rispettivamente quattro e una persona. Uno dei due conducenti era una donna di 82 anni.

items.title: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos
items.summary: The social media giant is accused of not informing 20 million users it had access to their photos.
items.content:
Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta €805m (£670m; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.

Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone users that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app.

It has given Meta, which also runs WhatsApp and Instagram, 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately.

The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech company.

The charge is related to a feature that suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts.

Facebook requested access to users' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. A preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery, according to the Italian regulator.

The regulator said it had taken into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact that the feature was "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".

It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation" in its decision.

Meta told the BBC: "We strongly disagree with the [regulator's] assessment of the facts, its application of the law and the disproportionate level of the fine.

"This is a straightforward feature which helps people post photos and videos to Facebook. People must give permission on their device before it can operate and they can change this permission at any time via their settings."

Last month, Meta was hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.

A judge in the US state of New Mexico ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) after it found that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

items.title: Philippines wins first Eurovision Song Contest Asia
items.summary: Front-runner Carmelle emerges victorious with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra.
items.content:
The Philippines have won the very first Eurovision Song Contest Asia, hosted in Bangkok and with 11 countries vying for the title.

Nineteen-year-old singer Carmelle was always a front runner with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra, complete with its catchy rap section.

She earned 211 points in total - 93 from the jury and 118 from the public vote - ahead of Thailand's MANG x DAOU in second place with 170 points.

There was a joyous atmosphere at the One Bangkok Arena as the crowd cheered the contestants and celebrated the popular winner.

Carmelle, the youngest contestant in the competition, was an obvious favourite with the juries and the public despite strong showings from several nations.

Other notable acts included MANG x DAOU, whose emotive duet Aroma elicited huge cheers from the home crowd.

Bangladeshi beatboxers Beatmosphere eschewed the traditional backing track, instead using their voices to replicate the sounds of drums and basslines.

And Laos's Thinla performed her crowd-pleasing song Bae in a traditional Lao hilltribe outfit.

However, the Laotian song had a unintentional second outing after the music video was played over an apparent technical issue during the broadcast - meaning it was the last song the audience heard before the vote.

The voting system worked much the same as the European Eurovison, with the public vote accounting for 50% of the result and the other 50% coming from the 11 national juries - with additional points awarded from a rest of the world vote.

Also performing during the broadcast was 2026 Eurovision Song Contest winner Dara from Bulgaria, who performed her winning song Bangaranga and new song Bad Idea.

Thai superstar Jeff Satur also made an appearance, hitting the high notes in his performance of Black Tie.

Eurovision in Asia was an idea that has been talked about for decades, but one that never seemed to materialise - despite many false starts - until now.

There is a huge enthusiasm here for Eurovision Asia, but a large number of the audience were established fans of the original contest from other countries and regions of the world.

Speaking after the show, fan Zelie Pereira - who travelled from Scotland to Thailand to attend - said she was "very happy" with Carmelle's win.

Korea, Vietnam and Laos also received praise from Pereira and her friends Michael Peters and Scarlett Massie, both from England.

"The dance was amazing. The sets were amazing. The costumes were amazing. The singing was amazing. Incredible", Peters added.

They confidently declared that "Asia Vision" should be the name for next year's show.

For some, it seems the excitement for another edition is already building.

However the crowd at the One Bangkok Arena thinned out not long after the Philippines singer Carmelle lifted the trophy.

The arena was crowded, but not full, and it's still not clear how much commitment there is among regional broadcasters to keep the contest going and expand it to more than 11 countries.

items.title: Sotheby's auction of $180m Van Gogh challenged over claims it was 'sold under duress'
items.summary: Sotheby's says it will work with the heirs of a family who had previously owned the artwork to try and reach a solution.
items.content:
Auction house Sotheby's says it is working to resolve a dispute over the intended sale of a painting by Vincent van Gogh.

Châtaigniers en fleurs ("Chestnut Trees in Blossom"), which carries an estimated value of $180m (£136m), is due to go under the hammer in New York on Wednesday.

But representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - say it may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

Sotheby's says its own "extensive research" has not established this, but that it will work with the family to try and reach a solution.

"Sotheby's takes provenance and restitution matters extremely seriously and has undertaken extensive research into the ownership history of Châtaigniers en fleurs," the auction house told the BBC in a statement.

"We are aware of the concerns recently raised by representatives of the Fischer heirs and have been in dialogue with them regarding the painting's history.

"While our research to date has not established that the painting was sold under duress, we recognise the importance of engaging thoughtfully and constructively with the family and are committed to working toward a mutually satisfactory resolution."

The painting is being sold as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.

Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.

It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.

The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotherby's says.

Four other owners have had it prior to it being put up for auction this year.

Fischer family heirs have instructed a lawyer who, according to the New York Times , external , has written to Sotherby's on their behalf.

He is said to have told the auction house the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis.

items.title: A family tree of software job titles
items.summary: Article URL: https://zwischenzugs.com/2026/11/03/a-family-tree-of-software-job-titles/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50499038 Points: 376 # Comments: 188
items.content:
For a few years I was ‘Head of DevOps’. Before I got that job title I’d done much the same work under other names, and since then I’ve watched the same work get called SRE, and then it seemed to morph towards platform engineering. If you’ve been in this industry for any length of time you’ll have seen titles come and go like this, and you might have wondered where they all came from.

So I (with the help of Mr Claude) built this family tree of software job titles, from the 1940s to now.

There are 104 titles, from ‘Computer’ (a person, not a machine) at the top to ‘AI Agent / Context Engineer’ at the bottom.

Time runs from top to bottom, in five-year rows. The titles sit in seven coloured columns by family:

A solid arrow means the title grew out of its parent. A dashed arrow means influence, or a common career move. Landmark titles are in bold.

On the site you can click a family to see just that column (here’s Data & AI ), or click a title to get its history, background and connections (here’s SRE ).

The whole thing is one Graphviz file and one JSON file of descriptions. Each title is one line in the .dot file, and the picture is rendered with:

Adding a title is three small edits: a node in its family’s column, an entry in the row for its five-year period, and its parent arrows.

A word on the dates. They’re roughly when a title became common , not its first recorded use, and they’re my best estimates, not sourced citations. Some are well known (SRE at Google in 2003, ‘DevOps’ coined in 2009, ‘Data Scientist’ in 2008). Plenty are a ‘c.’ and a shrug.

In 1947, Goldstine and von Neumann’s ‘Planning and Coding of Problems’ split the work of using a computer in two: mathematicians planned the problem, and coders translated the plan into machine instructions. Coding was treated as lower-status clerical work, and much of it was done by women.

It turned out that coding eventually became the hard, creative part, and the coder merged into the programmer.

Go back further and it’s stranger still. Several of the first ENIAC programmers were recruited from the Army’s human computers, people whose job was to compute by hand. So the job gave its name to the machine, and its people to programming.

The webmaster turned up around 1993, and was often a single person who wrote the HTML, ran the webserver (often a box under a desk), answered the email, and kept the site up (sometimes by kicking it, more often by plugging it back in after kicking it).

By the mid-2000s the title had all but gone, as it was unfashionably ancient. The code went to web developers, the servers to sysadmins, and the content to editors and designers.

Then the web developer split into front-end and back-end around 2005, and the two joined back up again as ‘full-stack’ around 2008.

This is the centralisation/distribution see-saw I’ve written about before , playing out in job titles.

The prompt engineer made headlines in 2023 with a few eye-wateringly well-paid job listings. As the models got better, the skill became part of other jobs, and on the tree it gets absorbed into the AI engineer almost as soon as it appears.

The scrum master is a slower version of the same story: demand peaked in the 2010s, and many organisations have since folded it back into engineering management or delivery roles.

The newest title on the tree is the ‘AI Agent / Context Engineer’ (c. 2025). The description for it currently says “time will tell whether it stays a separate title”. I’m not taking bets.

‘Systems Engineer’ is two different jobs on the tree. At IBM in the 1960s it was a pre-sales role, working with customers to design installations and get them running. In the 1990s, thanks largely to Microsoft’s MCSE certification, it meant a more senior, design-oriented sysadmin. Same title, different branch, no relation.

‘Configuration management’ started as a 1960s US defence discipline for tracking hardware changes, became software version control in the 1970s, and then came back decades later as the name for tools like Puppet and Chef.

The ‘forward deployed engineer’ (FDE) is one of the hottest titles of 2025, as OpenAI, Anthropic and plenty of AI startups hire FDEs to get AI working inside their customers’ organisations.

Palantir built its business around them from about 2010: software engineers embedded with a customer, often on site, building whatever is needed to make the product work for that customer’s problem.

Which sounds a lot like IBM’s systems engineers of the 1960s, who worked with customers before and after the sale, designing installations and getting systems running. (It also sounds a lot like old-style consulting, but I would say that.)

Ben Treynor Sloss defined SRE as “what happens when you ask a software engineer to design an operations team”. DevOps was meant as a culture of developers and operations working together, but by about 2011 ‘DevOps Engineer’ had become a job title, usually for whoever did the automation. On the tree, the arrow between SRE and DevOps points both ways. Platform engineering has both of them as parents, and was sold around 2022 as ‘the successor to DevOps’.

The Dev/Ops divide has never been resolved. It just keeps getting new names.

When I’m asked what the difference is between a DevOps engineer, an SRE and a platform engineer, the honest answer is always a little history lesson. This is the shortest version of that lesson I’ve managed so far.

The dates are best guesses, and I’ll have missed titles, mangled some lineages and drawn arrows people will argue with. If you know better, let me know, or raise a PR on the repo .

In 1947 coding was the clerical bit, and the real work was in the planning. Wind forward eighty years and you’ll hear much the same said about coding again, because AI. Last time, the coders turned out to be doing the hard part.

items.title: Lovable apps expose passport details and more than 200K private messages
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.crissyfield.de/research/lovable-en/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50499017 Points: 922 # Comments: 355
items.content:
AI makes it easier to build your own web applications, but handling sensitive data still requires special care. We examined 159,041 Lovable projects and found many cases where personal and confidential information was accessible without logging in.

Lovable is a Swedish AI startup founded in Stockholm in 2023 by Anton Osika and Fabian Hedin. The platform turns plain-language descriptions into web applications and is designed to be accessible even to people with little or no programming experience .

Lovable grew out of Osika's open-source project "GPT Engineer", released in 2023. The project evolved into the GPT Engineer App before being renamed Lovable in late 2024 and launching publicly that November.

Lovable can build impressively sophisticated web projects with AI, from static websites to full applications with user management and database connections. But as soon as an application handles confidential information, one question becomes crucial: Is that data protected against unauthorized access?

In its marketing , Lovable repeatedly emphasizes that no technical knowledge is needed to build projects . This can give the impression that the platform takes care of security too. Yet Lovable's Terms & Conditions place responsibility for applications and data handling on the customers themselves.

That leaves a troubling gap between the promise of an easy-to-use, all-in-one service and the responsibilities customers are expected to take on.

Against this backdrop, we investigated how well sensitive data in Lovable applications is protected, in collaboration with Handelsblatt . Lina Knees reported on the findings on November 2, 2026 (in German) .

We wanted to find out whether sensitive data in Lovable applications was accessible without logging in. We looked separately at data sent when a website first loaded and additional content we checked by making further read-only requests with the same API key.

The result: We found many clear examples of sensitive data left unprotected.

We focused on the database service Supabase . Its integration is relatively easy to analyze, and we believe it is the most widely used database service among Lovable projects. Lovable's own database features, introduced in late 2025, are still less widely used. Similar misconfigurations may occur there too, but we did not examine them in this analysis.

Using datasets from the open web archive Common Crawl , we identified and analyzed 159,041 Lovable projects from December 2025 to September 2026 . Of these, 34,545 used Supabase.

24,664 websites sent database records from Supabase as soon as they loaded, without requiring a login or any other interaction. That alone is not a security issue: the data may be intended for public display. But by making additional read-only requests, we were able to retrieve more database content. We found records containing email addresses in 10,560 tables across 7,403 of the 24,664 websites (30%).

Email addresses can help identify records containing personal data, but they may also be public contact addresses or test data. At the same time, this approach misses personal records that contain no email address. These effects partly offset one another, though we could not establish to what extent. The 30% figure should therefore not be read as a confirmed data leak rate. It applies only to the 24,664 websites we examined more closely. Our sample, drawn from Common Crawl, is also not representative of all Lovable applications.

We retrieved only parts of the datasets rather than downloading them in full. The figures below reflect the records we actually downloaded; the affected datasets may contain more. We are not publishing details of how to access them, as doing so could make further access easier.

A German lifestyle forum exposed more than 80,000 profiles containing full names, email addresses, dates of birth, and gender information. More than 200,000 chat messages were also accessible.

Several event organizers and restaurants exposed tens of thousands of records relating to ticket and food sales , with no login required. The records we inspected included email addresses, phone numbers, postal addresses, payment information, and ticket codes.

A property management company exposed AI-generated summaries of internal emails containing sensitive information about tenants, property owners, and business partners.

In a particularly serious case, a service provider exposed more than 1,000 records containing identity document details , including passport numbers , expiration dates , and nationalities . These highly sensitive identity details could be used for identity theft.

Other accessible content included tens of thousands of contracts , invoices , personal photo albums , and internal WhatsApp communications .

We also found numerous newsletter subscriptions, waiting lists, and contact and support inquiries. In one case, 280,000 emails sent to a provider's customers were accessible.

Depending on what it contains, exposed data like this could be used for phishing, ticket fraud, or identity theft. We could not establish whether any of it had been misused.

Handelsblatt contacted Lovable with the findings of our investigation.

Our analysis shows that many Lovable applications leave even highly sensitive data unprotected, with potentially serious consequences for the people affected.

Access control mistakes can happen in any application, whether written by people or built with AI. With Lovable, database integrations follow recurring patterns, making it easier for attackers to look for similar misconfigurations across many applications. An approach that works against one app may then work against others with little extra effort. Users without a technical background also face a harder task spotting and preventing these flaws.

An easy-to-use development platform does not remove the need for an expert review of access permissions before an application handles confidential data.

Automated checks are no substitute for a professional security assessment .

Before an application handles real customer or business data, its access permissions, interfaces, and separation between user accounts should be reviewed. These checks should be repeated after significant changes. If the necessary expertise is not available in-house, bring in qualified support.

If you would like help securing your application, please get in touch.

Note: This research report presents a more recent analysis and updated figures compared with the Handelsblatt article published on November 2, 2026.

Get in touch for an informal conversation. We'll look at your current situation and work with you to find the right solutions.

items.title: L’Alaska avrà il primo governatore Democratico dal 1998, e il più giovane della sua storia
items.content:
In Alaska è stato eletto il primo governatore Democratico dal 1998: è Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, già deputato statale per dieci anni e a 37 anni anche il più giovane nella storia dello stato. Sostituirà l’attuale governatore Mike Dunleavy. La vittoria è degna di nota perché l’Alaska è uno stato tradizionalmente Repubblicano : alle presidenziali vince stabilmente il candidato Repubblicano dal 1968 e oltre al governatore prima delle elezioni erano Repubblicani anche i due senatori e l’unico deputato (il conteggio per i seggi alle camere non è ancora finito).

L’elezione di Kreiss-Tomkins è stata annunciata più di 10 giorni dopo il giorno delle elezioni di metà mandato, perché in Alaska i voti per posta vengono contati se arrivano fino a 10 giorni dopo le elezioni. Kreiss-Tomkins si era presentato come un politico capace di unire gli elettori Democratici e Repubblicani per risolvere i problemi dell’Alaska, dove Donald Trump è impopolare. Proprio per questa sua caratteristica la sua candidatura era appoggiata da tre ex governatori di partiti diversi. Aveva anche puntato su restrizioni per i data center, un tema che quest’anno aveva messo d’accordo elettori di entrambi gli schieramenti.

Quest’anno delle elezioni di metà mandato in Alaska si era parlato soprattutto perché il Partito Democratico aveva candidato al Senato una persona con un nome quasi identico a quello del senatore uscente dei Repubblicani, Dan S. Sullivan. Solo che quest’uomo, Dan J. Sullivan, non c’entrava niente con la politica: era stato messo lì per confondere gli elettori e disperdere i voti.

items.title: WhatsApp come Instagram: sta arrivando la nuova funzione Instants
items.summary: Ecco cosa fa.
items.content:
Ad aprile Instagram ha lanciato "Instants" anche in Italia. E ora la stessa funzionalità sta per arrivare anche su WhatsApp. Come notato dal solito portale WaBetaInfo, infatti, nel codice della versione beta 2.26.45.13 di WhatsApp per Android è già possibile rintracciare tracce dei lavori in corso.

A quanto possiamo vedere oggi (tenendo conto che attualmente la feature non è disponibile neppure per i beta tester), un inedito pulsante contraddistinto dall'icona di un fulmine e collocato nella parte superiore della scheda Chat consentirà di aprire una fotocamera dedicata alla creazione e all'invio di contenuti effimeri (che andranno quindi ad affiancarsi ai messaggi effimeri di recente introduzione).

Da qui sarà possibile scattare foto o registrare video della durata massima di 30 secondi da condividere coi propri contatti. Non sarà possibile caricare immagini dalla galleria: come su Instagram, l'idea è quella di fornire uno strumento per condividere momenti estemporanei e destinati a scomparire dopo la visualizzazione.

items.title: Il riarmo europeo nasce dalla paura pesa la vicinanza della Russia
items.summary: Le industrie Ue devono allearsi e cambiare passo. Droni e Intelligenza artificiale si impadroniranno sempre di più dei campi di battaglia
items.content:
Il riarmo europeo ha un’accelerazione vertiginosa. Gli stanziamenti per la spesa militare lievitano , molto più che nel resto del mondo: si prevedono commesse per 1700 miliardi di euro entro il 2030 . Il boom non nasce dal rispetto dei parametri fissati dalla Nato, ma dalla paura: gli aumenti sono proporzionali alla prossimità geografica con l’Ucraina, come dimostra il picco di Polonia e Romania. Al timore di un confronto con la Russia si aggiunge la sfiducia nell’America di Donald Trump che obbliga a misurarsi con la necessità di difendersi da soli: un divorzio che secondo gli analisti proseguirà anche dopo la sconfitta repubblicana nel voto di midterm.

In queste nazioni, a partire dalla Germania, si è radicata la consapevolezza che in un pianeta dominato da rapporti di forza sia necessario tutelare a ogni costo la democrazia e il benessere che ha garantito. «Nel 1939 avevamo la ragione e il diritto dalla nostra parte ma si è visto come è andata a finire – ha dichiarato il ministro degli Esteri polacco Radoslaw Sikorski - . Adesso vogliamo essere pronti per lo scenario peggiore».

La priorità è il tempo: tutti i governi chiedono consegne rapide , che sono il requisito fondamentale pure per le esportazioni. Guardano alle lezioni che arrivano dall’Ucraina e dalla Russia, dove l’economia di guerra ogni sei-nove mesi progetta e schiera una nuova generazione di armamenti. La vera sfida non è tanto tecnologica quanto industriale. E non basta allargare gli impianti: ci vuole una rivoluzione della struttura produttiva. Le catene di montaggio di caccia o tank hanno ancora un’atmosfera dal sapore artigianale, con programmi decennali e componenti ordinate solo dopo la firma dei contratti: consegnano decine di esemplari l’anno, mentre ne vengono domandate centinaia. La svolta implica avere magazzini pieni e quindi filiere molto più robuste. In alcuni Paesi c’è l’impressione che la moltiplicazione delle commesse militari assorbirà l’eccesso di manodopera generato dalla crisi dell’automotive, cosa che sta avvenendo in Germania e su scala minore in Francia. In realtà si sta diffondendo la convinzione che il punto di arrivo della metamorfosi sia costruire armamenti come si fabbricano automobili , con gli stessi ritmi e la stessa velocità nell’aggiornare o personalizzare i modelli.

A complicare ulteriormente lo scenario c’è l’ingresso in scena di una categoria di concorrenti giovani e rampanti: aziende che non hanno origine nella manifattura meccanica ma in quella digitale. Sono quasi tutte statunitensi, raccolgono capitali illimitati e dispongono di relazioni solide con la Casa Bianca che gli hanno spalancato le porte del Pentagono. Anduril e Palantir sono le più note, tante altre stanno emergendo. Sono il Nuovo Testamento : gli evangelisti di un futuro dove droni e intelligenza artificiale si impadroniranno dei campi di battaglia in cielo, terra e mare. Promettono sistemi con prestazioni simili a quelli tradizionali, prezzi infimi e consegne lampo.

Sui due lati dell’Atlantico i Big finora hanno disdegnato i droni di “largo consumo” , adesso stanno cambiando idea. Nella Ue avviene per la pressione dei committenti: il vertice della Bundeswehr ha sostanzialmente imposto al colosso secolare Rheinmetall di produrre i cruise low cost della Destinus, fondata solo nel 2021. Anche Leonardo sta studiando come inserirsi in questa partita, che in Italia viene giocata da società intraprendenti ma poco strutturate tra cui Sky Eye, Siralab, General Defence, Xplora, Mirai, Alpi Aviation.

Nel panorama europeo il gruppo di Piazza Montegrappa è stato il primo a concepire una visione di lungo respiro, che unisce l’espansione continentale alla tutela della sovranità tecnologica e produttiva. La chiave sono le alleanze, forgiate nella gestione di Stefano Cingolani e che ora l’amministratore delegato Lorenzo Mariani sta rendendo operative. Il caccia di sesta generazione Gcap portato avanti con Regno Unito e Giappone – a cui guardano con interesse Germania e Canada – è il laboratorio di innovazioni che ricadono a cascata sugli sviluppi dell’Eurofighter e della radaristica.

L’intesa con Rheinmetall e l’acquisto di Iveco Defence Vehicles, storico partner di Oto Melara, hanno reso Leonardo uno dei leader globali nei mezzi corazzati cingolati e ruotati. Strumenti che verranno trasformati con l’inserimento dell’elettronica, punto di forza della compagnia, per farne la centrale mobile di uno sciame di automi volanti e terrestri. La stessa idea ispira l’accordo con Baycar, il prodigio turco dei droni di fascia alta: saranno integrati con sensori e apparati made in Italy, offrendo l’unico sistema europeo della categoria. Infine c’è lo spazio: il patto con Airbus e Thales è ai blocchi di partenza in attesa del via libera di Bruxelles.

La filosofia di Mariani è quella che ha maturato ai vertici di Mbda, l’unica realtà continentale: la strada per restare protagonisti è coalizzare i campioni nazionali in una dimensione europea. Contemporaneamente, c’è l’urgenza di farsi carico dell’irrobustimento della filiera di piccole e medie imprese da cui dipende il potenziamento delle catene di montaggio. È una rotta obbligata, simile a quella intrapresa da Pierroberto Folgiero di Fincantieri, Renzo Tosini di Mbda e Domitilla Benigni di Elt, declinandola a seconda delle specializzazioni e intensificando i rapporti tra loro. Fincantieri e Leonardo lo hanno testimoniato a inizio novembre con la lettera d’intenti firmata nel salone parigino Euronaval.

La sintonia più difficile, soprattutto in Italia, è quella con i governi, a cui le aziende domandano più certezze sui programmi, approvati e poi spesso paralizzati da calcoli politici ed elettorali. Sono le dinamiche delle democrazie. Nella nostra la sicurezza nazionale non è all’ordine del giorno e questo determina uno svantaggio competitivo per le industrie della difesa.
